strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gaps in sign language translation: fingerspelling under-representation and asynchronous non-manual cues, with clear articulation of specific challenges (temporal blurring, visual ambiguity, data imbalance)
Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over prior SOTA: BLEU-4 23.5 (vs. 15.5), fingerspelling letter accuracy 73.2% (vs. 71.1%), and sequence classification 99.2%

Comprehensive ablation studies systematically evaluating component contributions (modality-specific predictors, LLM sizing, glossing methods, temporal alignment), providing useful insights into driver of performance
Principled modular architecture with learned temporal fusion explicitly addressing asynchronicity between manual and non-manual modalities—a real challenge in sign language

Appropriate experimental setup with proper dataset splits, multiple metrics (Letter Accuracy, BLEU, ROUGE), and supplementary qualitative analysis including failure cases and modality routing visualizations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (ViT, CTC, transformer gating) without introducing new methods; fusion mechanism (Eq. 10-11) uses simple element-wise gating rather than sophisticated cross-modal attention

Critical technical clarity gaps: (1) hard Gumbel-Softmax routing's gradient flow during training unexplained; (2) pseudo-glossing method vague—LLM Glossing performance identical to full model (23.5 BLEU) suggesting confounding; (3) learned alignment mechanism (Table 6) underspecified; (4) loss weighting scheme missing from Eq. 17

Severely limited evaluation scope: only ASL tested despite paper motivating BSL and DGS; unsupported claims of 'robust, high-fidelity translation' lacking cross-dataset evaluation; no generalization testing to different signers/contexts beyond training data

Lipreading integration mechanism opaque: unclear why mouth movements help fingerspelling letter recognition (54.3%→73.2%); hypothesis that lip cues disambiguate homonymous handshapes (M vs. N) stated without evidence; conceptual confusion between mouthings and facial expressions

Reproducibility severely compromised: no code/model release mentioned; missing hyperparameters (dropout, layer widths, learning rates); staged training procedure details sparse; no confidence intervals or significance testing; computational cost analysis absent despite multi-component architecture
Modest absolute performance: BLEU-4 of 23.5 remains low for practical sentence translation; limited error analysis with only 2 failure cases; no systematic categorization of failure modes
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Llava-SLT mentioned but not compared; SSVP-SLT (prior SOTA) unexplained; missing comparisons with recent multimodal fusion methods from 2024-2025

Staged training procedure potentially suboptimal: frozen predictors during fusion stage; no comparison with end-to-end fine-tuning justifying this design choice; concern that solution lies in local optimum rather than global
Temporal alignment asymmetry (Table 6) unexplained: negative shifts hurt less than positive shifts—why are manual signals leading lip movements more natural? Questions fundamental design assumptions

Evaluation limited to single domain/scale: How2Sign only (11 signers, ~35K clips); YouTube-ASL used for pretraining but not evaluation; no cross-dataset evaluation (RWTH-PHOENIX, LSF, etc.); generalization beyond instructional videos untested

strengths: Strong empirical results with consistent improvements across multiple datasets (How2Sign +6.6 BLEU-4, BOBSL +4.2, ChicagoFSWildPlus +2.1%), demonstrating the effectiveness of the modular approach
Well-motivated problem formulation grounded in sign language linguistics, identifying fingerspelling and temporal non-manual misalignment as critical challenges
Sound architectural design with principled choices: gated fusion (O(T) complexity), CTC loss for alignment, staged training to prevent gradient conflicts, and specialized expert networks

Comprehensive experimental validation including detailed ablations (component importance, fusion strategies, temporal alignment, LLM size), fine-grained POS analysis, and zero-shot generalization studies
Excellent reproducibility with extensive supplementary material including hyperparameters, training details, pseudo-glossing pipeline, and qualitative examples from each modality stream
Linguistically grounded analysis revealing model strengths on content words (NOUN 0.47, PROPN 0.56) and systematic weaknesses on function words, enabling future improvements
Data contribution of pseudo-gloss and phoneme annotations for 1.5M BOBSL and 35k How2Sign sentences
weaknesses: Critical dependency on GPT-4o–generated pseudo-glosses without validation: no human evaluation of linguistic quality, no verification against ASL conventions, and no analysis of whether this proxy adequately represents Deaf signer conventions

Significant and unmitigated underperformance on function words (determiners 0.38 vs. baselines ~0.44, conjunctions 0.24 vs. 0.42) representing a fundamental limitation inadequately addressed or explained
High computational cost (240 GPU-hours training, 30-60 min inference per test set) with no implemented solutions, creating deployment barriers for an accessibility-critical application
Absence of user validation: no evaluation with Deaf signers or native sign language users, and no human judgment studies on translation fluency/adequacy despite claiming accessibility benefits
Limited temporal alignment analysis: learned offsets demonstrated to outperform fixed shifts (Table 7) but not interpreted or visualized; no cross-dataset validation
Generalization limited to two sign languages (ASL, BSL) with no evaluation on DGS or others; pseudo-gloss prompt explicitly targets ASL structure, limiting transferability claims

Model capacity confound: comparison benefits from increased capacity (197.5M visual + 6.7B LLM vs. some baselines with 580M-680M LM), making architectural contribution unclear without capacity-controlled ablation
Domain-specific overfitting evidenced by high interjection accuracy (0.73) attributed to dataset bias toward instructional videos with conventional openers ('Alright', 'Okay')
Incomplete error analysis: two failure modes identified (proper noun hallucination, semantic drift) but not quantified; prevalence and severity unknown

Modest novelty in individual components (parallel experts, gated fusion, LLM refinement exist separately; pseudo-gloss generation relies on existing LLM capabilities) despite solid engineering integration

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gaps in SLT (fingerspelling, non-manual cues) grounded in sign language linguistics
Strong empirical results across three datasets (How2Sign: +6.6 BLEU-4, ChicagoFSWildPlus: 73.2% letter acc., BOBSL: +4.2 BLEU-4)
Comprehensive ablation studies including temporal alignment analysis, fusion architecture comparison, and fine-grained POS-level linguistic analysis
Detailed supplementary material with implementation details, hyperparameters, and qualitative examples supporting reproducibility efforts
Evaluation on multiple datasets (How2Sign, ChicagoFSWildPlus, BOBSL) with attention to cross-linguistic generalization (ASL/BSL)
weaknesses: Critical methodological flaw: visual experts trained on GPT-4o pseudo-glosses (not human annotations), then LLM trained on same (gloss, English) pairs, creating circular dependency. Improvements may reflect LLM consistency with itself, not improved visual understanding. Pseudo-gloss quality never validated.

Unfair baseline comparisons: baselines lack access to GPT-4o pseudo-gloss supervision that SignBind-LLM receives. Improvements attributable to additional training signal, not architectural superiority.

Limited technical novelty: standard components (DINOv2 backbone, ViT, LLaMA-2), simple gating mechanism (Eq. 12), straightforward Gumbel-softmax routing. Engineering integration rather than novel methodology.

Weak visual understanding with heavy LLM dependence: continuous signing alone yields only 6.3 BLEU-4; removing LLM drops from 22.1 to 7.8 BLEU-4 (~65% of final performance comes from LLM refinement). Visual pipeline is largely a noisy pseudo-gloss generator.
No human evaluation: relies solely on automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE) which are poor proxies for SLT quality. Prior SLT work used human evaluation; this omission is problematic.

Function word accuracy regresses: determiners 0.38 vs 0.43-0.45 (baselines), conjunctions 0.24 vs 0.41-0.42, particles 0.43 vs 0.56-0.61. Paper's own POS analysis reveals grammatical degradation not adequately discussed.
Impractical inference speed: 30 min to 1 hour per test set on RTX 4090; unusable for live interpretation. Paper acknowledges but dismisses ('beyond scope'), with no optimization attempts.

Pseudo-glosses not released/validated: claims to provide 1.5M BOBSL and 35k How2Sign pseudo-gloss annotations but unclear if released; no analysis of coverage, accuracy, or linguistic validity relative to human glosses.
Fingerspelling evaluation limited to isolated sequences: ChicagoFSWildPlus tests isolated fingerspelling, not embedded in continuous signing where temporal asynchrony is most relevant.
Missing human evaluation, fair baseline comparisons, statistical significance tests, released code/pseudo-glosses, and adequate justification of inference latency for practical deployment.

strengths: Well-motivated multi-modal architecture addressing genuine limitations in SLT: temporal asynchrony between manual and non-manual signals, fingerspelling, and mouthings
Strong empirical results across three diverse datasets with substantial improvements (+6.6 BLEU-4 on How2Sign, +4.2 BLEU-4 on BOBSL, +2.1pp on ChicagoFSWildPlus)

Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablations, POS-level linguistic analysis revealing content word strengths and function word weaknesses, temporal shift studies, and zero-shot generalization
Principled staged training approach with learned gating mechanisms for handling temporal asynchrony between hand and mouth movements—addresses real linguistic co-articulation phenomena
Excellent supplementary material enabling reproducibility with complete hyperparameters, architectural details, training procedures, and qualitative examples
Addresses important accessibility need for Deaf communities with clear societal impact
Qualitative analysis (Tables 17-18) demonstrates how each expert contributes and how fusion resolves ambiguities
weaknesses: Critical dependence on GPT-4o for pseudo-gloss generation undermines reproducibility: requires proprietary API, introduces black-box dependency, and lacks validation of pseudo-gloss quality or error impact analysis

Significant performance gaps on function words (Determiners: 0.38, CCONJ: 0.24, Particles: 0.43) that impact grammatical correctness; visual-centric approach has acknowledged architectural limits with no proposed solutions
Complex multi-stage training with frozen parameters at each stage leaves optimization gaps—no exploration of whether end-to-end joint fine-tuning after staged pre-training provides additional gains
High computational cost: 240 GPU-hours training time and 30 minutes to 1 hour inference per test set limits practical deployment and reproducibility

Parameter scale confounds comparison: 6935.9M total parameters (vs ~600M for competitors); unclear whether improvements from visual architecture or simply using larger LLaMA-7B vs smaller LMs used in baselines
Limited error analysis: only two primary failure modes identified without systematic study; no confidence calibration despite identifying unreliable predictions
Lipreading signal quality concern: 65.6% phoneme accuracy yet shown to be most critical component, suggesting potential over-weighting of weak signals or underperformance of continuous sign expert
Limited generalization scope: only ASL/BSL evaluated; no other sign languages tested; only indoor/controlled signing; English-only target language
Pseudo-gloss 'annotations' for BOBSL and How2Sign are unvalidated GPT-4o outputs, not linguistic annotations, potentially introducing LLM artifacts into datasets

Technical details lack clarity: adaptive gate α appears to be scalar per timestep (suboptimal vs element-wise); Gumbel-Softmax temperature during inference not discussed; upsampling T' to T not justified
